scenarios.title: Read an IPv4 address
scenarios.summary: Find the subnet boundaries and choose an unused address for a second workstation.
scenarios.objective: A workstation is configured as 192.168.10.77/27. Determine its network address, broadcast address, and usable host range, then assign a valid, different address to a second workstation.
steps: Complete the subnet assignment in the native address fields. Optional hints explain the block size and the network/host boundary.
Enter the network and broadcast addresses. Keep the same network bits when finding both boundaries.
Enter both usable endpoints and a different usable address for workstation 2. Check configuration grades all five fields.
hints: /27 leaves five host bits, so each block holds 32 addresses.
In this example the first three octets stay fixed; last-octet blocks start at multiples of 32.
Reserve the first and last addresses for network and broadcast. The second workstation must also avoid the address already in use.
scenarios.simplifications: Conventional broadcast subnets only; /31 point-to-point and /32 host routes are excluded.

guide.title: Read the prefix
guide.why: A /27 fixes 27 network bits and leaves five host bits. Each block contains 2⁵ = 32 addresses.
guide.action: Complete the subnet assignment in the native address fields. Optional hints explain the block size and the network/host boundary.

guide.title: Mark both boundaries
guide.why: The network has all host bits zero; the broadcast has all host bits one. Neither is assigned to a conventional host.
guide.action: Enter the network and broadcast addresses. Keep the same network bits when finding both boundaries.

guide.title: Identify usable hosts
guide.why: The first usable host follows the network, and the last precedes the broadcast.
guide.action: Enter both usable endpoints and a different usable address for workstation 2. Check configuration grades all five fields.

scenarios.explanation: A /27 leaves five host bits: 32 addresses per block. The block containing .77 starts at .64 and ends at .95. The network is 192.168.10.64, broadcast is 192.168.10.95, and usable hosts run from .65 through .94 (30 hosts).

address_teaching.prerequisite_note: Start here even if you have never used binary. Type addresses into the labeled fields; Check configuration checks your choices. Your original assignment and example stay separate.

concepts.title: A computer belongs to an address group
concepts.text: An IPv4 address has four numbers from 0 to 255, separated by dots. The full address identifies a computer’s interface. Its subnet is the group of addresses treated as local neighbors. The subnet mask describes that grouping; it is a rule, not another computer’s address.

concepts.title: A prefix determines the block size
concepts.text: IPv4 has 32 on/off positions, called bits. /26 keeps 26 for the network and leaves 6 host bits. Each has two choices, so 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 64 addresses per block. A larger prefix leaves fewer host bits and makes smaller blocks.

concepts.title: Find the block containing this computer
concepts.text: In this /26 example, blocks start at 0, 64, 128 and 192 in the last number. 139 is at least 128 and below the next start, 192, so it lies in 128–191. Keep the earlier numbers: the network is 192.168.5.128, broadcast is 192.168.5.191, and usable hosts are 192.168.5.129 through 192.168.5.190. The first and last addresses are reserved in this exercise.

address_teaching.example_description: Try 192.168.5.139/26 in a separate practice example. Its subnet mask is 255.255.255.192; the mask describes the grouping, while 192.168.5.139 is the computer’s address. The graded assignment uses a different address and /27. Optional prefix help explains boundaries in earlier numbers. This exercise excludes /31 and /32.
address_teaching.try_change: Fill the worked example, check it, then give Workstation 2 another free address between 129 and 190 while avoiding 139. Try 191 next and read why it cannot be assigned. The assignment remains untouched.

scenarios.title: Give each team a subnet
scenarios.summary: Divide one address pool without overlapping networks.
scenarios.objective: Allocate aligned subnets within 10.20.0.0/24 for design (60 hosts), support (28) and lab (12). Larger valid allocations are accepted if all fit without overlap.
steps: In the allocation table, give design enough addresses for 60 hosts plus network and broadcast.
Enter aligned network/prefix values for support and lab. The Hosts column lists each team’s minimum requirement.
Check work evaluates capacity, alignment, containment and overlap. Review the row results and adjust your plan.
hints: A /26 holds 62 usable hosts, /27 holds 30, and /28 holds 14.
One layout is design at .0/26, support at .64/27, lab at .96/28. Other valid layouts work.
scenarios.simplifications: No routing or DHCP modeling. Conventional subnets reserve two addresses.

guide.title: Size the largest team first
guide.why: Include two reserved addresses in every conventional subnet. Starting with the largest avoids leaving unusable fragments.
guide.action: In the allocation table, give design enough addresses for 60 hosts plus network and broadcast.

guide.title: Place the remaining teams
guide.why: Subnet boundaries must align to their block sizes. Each allocation must be inside the pool without sharing addresses.
guide.action: Enter aligned network/prefix values for support and lab. The Hosts column lists each team’s minimum requirement.

guide.title: Check the whole plan
guide.why: A plan can have sufficient capacity and still fail because two allocations overlap. More than one layout is valid.
guide.action: Check work evaluates capacity, alignment, containment and overlap. Review the row results and adjust your plan.

scenarios.explanation: 60 hosts require at least /26 (62 usable), 28 require /27 (30 usable), and 12 require /28 (14 usable). One plan is 10.20.0.0/26, 10.20.0.64/27 and 10.20.0.96/28. Other aligned, disjoint plans within the /24 are equally valid.

address_teaching.prerequisite_note: First use the subnet lesson’s network, broadcast and usable-host ideas. Here you plan several address groups inside one supplied pool. An allocation is simply one team’s chosen subnet.

concepts.title: Count all addresses, then reserve two
concepts.text: Each team needs room for its computers plus network and broadcast addresses. A /28 has 16 addresses and 14 usable hosts; a /27 has 32 addresses and 30 usable hosts. For 30 hosts, /28 is too small. Choose a block size such as 8, 16, 32 or 64 addresses—each size doubles—with enough usable places. These are powers of two.

concepts.title: Start on a real boundary
concepts.text: A block must begin at one of its own boundaries. In a /24 pool, /27 blocks begin at last numbers 0, 32, 64 and so on; /29 blocks begin at 0, 8, 16 and so on. Starting a /27 at 10 does not create a new boundary. Type its network/prefix, not an individual host address.

concepts.title: Fit distinct groups inside the pool
concepts.text: Give the largest requirement space first, then place smaller aligned blocks in unused space. Every block must stay inside the supplied pool and must not overlap another team. This is variable-length subnet masking, or VLSM: different teams can use different block sizes. Larger-than-minimum valid blocks are allowed if everything still fits.

address_teaching.example_description: In a separate 192.0.2.0/24 pool, plan for Staff 30 hosts and Visitors 6 hosts. A /27 supplies 30 usable places; a /29 supplies 6. The example table shows the chosen network/prefix for each team, and Check example verifies capacity, boundaries, containment and overlap.
address_teaching.try_change: After checking the example, move Visitors to 192.0.2.64/29 and check again: another free aligned block is valid. Then try 192.0.2.8/29 and inspect the overlap with Staff. Restore a separate block before opening the assignment.

scenarios.title: Reconnect the office client
scenarios.summary: Repair a client mask and default route.
scenarios.objective: Keep client address 192.168.40.70. Match the router LAN /26, use gateway 192.168.40.65, and reach remote server 203.0.113.10.
steps: Inspect the client’s current mask and default route.
Replace the single simulated interface address.
Update the default route, then test the remote server.
hints: A /26 here places the client and router in 192.168.40.64/26.
Use ip addr set 192.168.40.70/26 and ip route replace default via 192.168.40.65.
scenarios.simplifications: Abstract topology; no ARP, packet forwarding, latency, switches or ICMP filtering. Commands are a documented teaching subset.

guide.title: Compare the client with its router
guide.why: The LAN prefix determines which addresses are on-link. A default route must point to a router on that LAN.
guide.action: Inspect the client’s current mask and default route.

commands.explanation: Shows the client prefix and the router’s LAN prefix.
Shows the client’s default gateway.

guide.title: Correct the client prefix
guide.why: The router uses /26. The client must keep its assigned .70 address and use the same LAN prefix.
guide.action: Replace the single simulated interface address.

commands.explanation: Teaching shortcut: replaces the modeled client interface; this is not full iproute2 syntax.

guide.title: Choose the router and verify
guide.why: Remote traffic needs the reachable LAN router as its next hop. A successful ping tests this modeled path.
guide.action: Update the default route, then test the remote server.

commands.explanation: Uses the LAN router as the default next hop.
Tests reachability to the simulated remote server.

scenarios.explanation: The client .70 and router .65 share 192.168.40.64/26. Keeping .70/26 and routing remote traffic via .65 restores this modeled path. A /24 mask would incorrectly treat additional addresses as on-link.

client_teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on Read an IPv4 address. Keep a workstation’s assigned address while applying the supplied LAN prefix and choosing its local router; no new subnet calculation is required here.

concepts.title: Address and prefix have different jobs
concepts.text: The address identifies this client. The prefix describes its local group. Follow the supplied LAN plan while keeping the client’s assigned address; changing the gateway does not change that address.

concepts.title: A default gateway is the next hop
concepts.text: For a destination outside the local group, this task uses the supplied LAN router as its default next hop. The remote target is a different address reached through that router, not the value to enter as the gateway.

concepts.title: Apply, then inspect
concepts.text: Fields are saved drafts until Apply client settings changes this virtual client. The diagram shows applied values. ip addr and ip route give compact simulated views; the router’s plan is supplied context, not information a real ip addr command discovers. The retained ip addr set form is an older simulator editor shortcut, not full Linux syntax.

concepts.title: Test the local and remote paths separately
concepts.text: A reply from the LAN router does not prove the required remote setup is correct. Try ping with the supplied router and target addresses, then Check work for all three requirements. These are abstract path checks, without ARP, packet forwarding or real ICMP.

client_teaching.example_description: A different client is assigned 198.51.100.150. Its supplied LAN router is 198.51.100.129/27 and remote target is 203.0.113.90. Repair the current /24 prefix and .1 gateway without changing .150. Practice is separate from the office assignment.

example_actions.title: Inspect the client
example_actions.explanation: Read the current address/prefix alongside the supplied router LAN plan. This query changes no settings.

command.explanation: Compact simulated client view; not a complete real iproute2 dump.

example_actions.title: Inspect the default route
example_actions.explanation: Compare the current next hop with the supplied router. This query changes no settings.

command.explanation: Shows the one modeled default gateway.

example_actions.title: Apply the example LAN plan
example_actions.explanation: Insert fills the three example fields only: keep .150, use /27 and choose .129 as gateway. Press Apply client settings to apply them to the example.

example_actions.title: Test the remote target
example_actions.explanation: Run this path check after applying the example settings. A simulated reply checks this particular target, not full network or application behavior.

command.explanation: Checks the abstract remote path in this example; no real packet or host command runs.

client_teaching.try_change: After the example passes, change only Default gateway to 198.51.100.130 and Apply. ping 198.51.100.129 can still reply locally, but ping 203.0.113.90 is unreachable. Check example shows the route still needs work. Restore gateway .129 and Apply to repair the example.

scenarios.title: Share a report safely
scenarios.summary: Give Alex read/write access while keeping the file private.
scenarios.objective: Let alex read and write /srv/report.txt; give other users no permissions on that file.
steps: Compare the file’s ownership and permissions with alex’s groups.
Change the file mode. An ownership-based solution can also work.
Inspect the repaired mode, then optionally use the simulator’s access probe.
hints: alex belongs to editors. Group bits need read (4) plus write (2).
chmod 660 /srv/report.txt gives owner/group read-write and no other permissions.
scenarios.simplifications: Administrator mutations; test-access uses ordinary POSIX owner/group/other precedence. No ACLs, root override, special mode bits or SELinux. Privacy excludes the root administrator; all other modeled users and the other permission class are checked. Group access is valid only while no other modeled user can use it.

guide.title: Read owner and group access
guide.why: POSIX chooses one permission class: owner first, then a matching group, otherwise other.
guide.action: Compare the file’s ownership and permissions with alex’s groups.

commands.explanation: Reads the symbolic mode, owner and group columns.
Shows primary and supplementary group memberships.

guide.title: Give Alex the required access
guide.why: Alex belongs to editors. Group read/write works here only while no other modeled non-administrator user can use that access. Changing ownership to Alex and removing group permissions is another valid solution.
guide.action: Change the file mode. An ownership-based solution can also work.

commands.explanation: Gives owner and group read/write; leaves other users no file permissions.

guide.title: Verify effective access
guide.why: Correct file bits alone are insufficient if a parent directory cannot be traversed.
guide.action: Inspect the repaired mode, then optionally use the simulator’s access probe.

commands.explanation: Confirms the resulting permission bits.
Simulator-only probe of alex’s effective access through the full path.

scenarios.explanation: With root as owner and editors as group, mode 660 gives alex group read/write and removes all other-class permissions. Changing ownership to alex while retaining restrictive bits is another valid solution. Owner permissions take precedence over group permissions.

legacy_access_teaching.prerequisite_note: Use the inspect-and-repair method from Access policy and safe file changes. This older exercise gives you a virtual administrator role; it does not operate on your computer.

concepts.title: Choose one permission class
concepts.text: Every entry has an owner and a group. ls -l /srv/brief.txt shows its owner, group and read/write/execute bits. The model chooses owner bits when the user owns the entry; otherwise matching group bits; otherwise other bits. These classes are not added together. id dana shows Dana belongs to reviewers.

concepts.title: Translate the requested access
concepts.text: Read is 4, write is 2 and execute is 1 in an octal mode digit. On the practice file, chmod 660 /srv/brief.txt gives owner and reviewers read/write and gives the other class no bits. Dana uses group bits while root owns it. Changing ownership to Dana and using 600 is another possible method; neither an exact mode nor one repair order is a hidden goal.

concepts.title: Verify the user, not only the listing
concepts.text: test-access dana /srv/brief.txt rw is a simulator-only probe, not a Linux utility. It checks parent search permission and file access for Dana. Here mutations are administrative even when an ordinary user could not change the file. Privacy excludes the root administrator but also checks other modeled people: the unrelated observer must not gain access.

concepts.title: Know this small terminal
concepts.text: Type one explained command and choose Run or Enter. Insert action fills the input only. This older terminal uses exact absolute paths and whitespace tokens, without shell quoting or expansion. It has no ACL, special mode bits or root access override. Practice remains separate; later Check work grades the full assignment from its current access state.

legacy_access_teaching.example_description: Give dana read/write access to /srv/brief.txt, keeping the file private from the other class and every modeled nonadministrator except Dana. root owns it and reviewers is its group; Dana already belongs to reviewers. Inspect, change and probe this separate example.

commands.explanation: Read the compact mode, owner and group columns before changing anything.
Read the modeled primary and supplementary groups; displayed numeric IDs are derived labels, not account-management records.
Give owner and reviewers read/write while removing other-class bits.
Probe Dana's effective read/write access in this simulator.
The unrelated observer should remain denied in this simulator.

legacy_access_teaching.try_change: After success, run chmod 440 /srv/brief.txt and probe Dana for rw. Removing write makes the current access check fail. Restore 660 for the group-based method, then probe and Check example again.

scenarios.title: Unlock the project directory
scenarios.summary: Trace group access through a directory tree.
scenarios.objective: Give blair read access to /srv/project/notes.txt without public file permissions. Repair group membership and traversal as needed.
steps: Inspect both blair’s groups and each component of the file path.
Add editors without replacing existing groups. This model refreshes sessions immediately.
Give editors directory traversal, then verify access to the file.
hints: Directory read lists names; execute allows traversal. Both can be useful, but traversal is necessary here.
usermod -aG editors blair followed by chmod 750 /srv/project repairs this path.
scenarios.simplifications: No supplementary-group session refresh, ACLs or SELinux. Alternative ownership/permission repairs are accepted if effective access and privacy hold.

guide.title: Trace the entire path
guide.why: Reading a file requires search/execute on every parent directory, plus read on the file.
guide.action: Inspect both blair’s groups and each component of the file path.

commands.explanation: Checks whether blair belongs to the file’s group.
Shows the modeled owner, group and mode at every path component.

guide.title: Add the missing group
guide.why: Supplementary group membership allows the group permission class to apply.
guide.action: Add editors without replacing existing groups. This model refreshes sessions immediately.

commands.explanation: Appends editors to blair’s supplementary groups.

guide.title: Restore directory traversal
guide.why: Directory read lists names; directory execute permits access through the directory.
guide.action: Give editors directory traversal, then verify access to the file.

commands.explanation: Gives the editors group read and search on the project directory.
Simulator-only effective read-access probe.

scenarios.explanation: Adding blair to editors permits the group class to apply. Mode 750 on /srv/project adds the execute/search bit missing from 740. The file’s existing group-read bit then becomes reachable through all parent directories. Effective-access alternatives are accepted.

legacy_access_teaching.prerequisite_note: Use Share a report safely to choose owner/group/other permissions. This independent example adds a path with more than one directory. It keeps its own users, modes and command history.

concepts.title: Every parent needs search
concepts.text: Reading a known file needs search/execute on every directory leading to it, including /, then read permission on the file. Directory read lists names; search lets a user pass through a known path. Missing search can block a readable file. Here namei /srv/review/plan.txt gives a compact simulated octal-mode/owner/group view, not the full real namei output.

concepts.title: Membership and bits are separate
concepts.text: id evan initially lacks inspectors. usermod -aG inspectors evan appends one existing group and keeps Evan's primary group. This administrative simulation refreshes membership immediately; real existing login sessions may need refreshing. It does not create accounts/groups or model credentials. All group names must already exist in the supplied membership lists.

concepts.title: Add only what access needs
concepts.text: The directory starts 740: group read without search. After adding inspectors, chmod 710 /srv/review gives the group search without requiring listing or write. The existing 640 file then supplies group read. 750 also works; exact directory read/write bits are not requested. Inspections are administrative; use test-access to ask about Evan's effective access.

concepts.title: Public is not the same as exclusive
concepts.text: This task removes the file's other-class permissions; it does not ban an existing teammate who belongs to inspectors. test-access evan /srv/review/plan.txt r is a simulator-only check. In the full assignment Blair must gain read access without public file bits; existing Alex/editor access can remain. Current effective access, not a membership-change history, is graded.

legacy_access_teaching.example_description: Let evan read /srv/review/plan.txt without public file permissions. Add the existing inspectors group and repair parent search as needed. The existing colleague may retain access. This example is independent of Blair's project assignment.

commands.explanation: Inspect the current group list before changing it.
Inspect compact simulated path components; this is not a full namei output/options model.
Append the known group; simulated sessions update immediately.
Give inspectors search on the directory. Listing and write are not required here.
Simulator-only probe of Evan's read access through all parents.

legacy_access_teaching.try_change: After success, run chmod 700 /srv/review. The file still has group-read bits, but Evan loses parent search. Probe r and Check example, then restore 710 (or 750) and verify the path again.

scenarios.title: Find the failing requests
scenarios.summary: Locate a log and extract the relevant lines.
scenarios.objective: Find app.log under /var/log, then produce exactly its ERROR lines as the last text query.

files./var/log/app.log:
09:00 INFO startup ready
09:02 ERROR database unavailable
09:03 INFO retry scheduled
09:04 ERROR request timeout
09:05 WARN queue growing

steps: Locate app.log under /var/log.
Read the application log.
Produce both ERROR lines as the last text query. A later unfiltered query will change the graded result.
hints: grep takes a one-word literal and a path; pipelines can also filter cat output.
grep ERROR /var/log/app.log produces both requested lines.
scenarios.simplifications: Literal case-sensitive matching only; no regex, globbing, quoting, redirection or general shell. find only searches the simulated log map.

guide.title: Locate the log
guide.why: Finding the correct file prevents filtering unrelated messages. All paths here belong to the simulated filesystem.
guide.action: Locate app.log under /var/log.

commands.explanation: Searches the simulated log catalog for that file name.

guide.title: Read before filtering
guide.why: Inspect the message format to choose a literal that isolates the requested severity.
guide.action: Read the application log.

commands.explanation: Prints the modeled log, including INFO, WARN and ERROR lines.

guide.title: Extract just the errors
guide.why: grep retains matching lines. This documented subset matches a case-sensitive one-word literal.
guide.action: Produce both ERROR lines as the last text query. A later unfiltered query will change the graded result.

commands.explanation: Prints only the lines containing ERROR.
An alternate pipeline that produces the same result.

scenarios.explanation: Both ERROR lines must be retained and the INFO/WARN lines excluded. Direct grep or cat piped into grep produces the same resulting text. The most recent successful text query is graded, so printing the unfiltered log afterward removes current completion.

legacy_logs_teaching.prerequisite_note: Use the inspect-then-change method from Files, paths and safe handovers. This older log exercise has a small fixed catalog; its find and filter forms are simpler than the later recursive-search and script units.

concepts.title: Locate and inspect the supplied text
concepts.text: A log is a sequence of text lines describing events. find /var/log -name worker.log locates that exact basename in this supplied catalog. It does not use wildcard patterns, depth or directory permissions. cat /var/log/worker.log displays the whole log. All paths are virtual; no host log is read.

concepts.title: Filter a literal substring
concepts.text: grep FAIL /var/log/worker.log keeps each line containing the case-sensitive text FAIL. This exercise treats one word literally, not as a regular expression or a severity-field parser. FAIL and fail differ. There are two requested FAIL lines and INFO/WARN lines to exclude. The separate audit log has different messages; inspect the right source.

concepts.title: Pass text through a pipeline
concepts.text: cat /var/log/worker.log | grep FAIL produces the same selected text. A pipe passes one stage's output to the next. Put spaces around | in this small terminal. There is no shell quoting, expansion, redirection or general command evaluator. tail -n 3 /var/log/worker.log inspects recent lines but can omit an earlier failure; filtering the full log avoids that omission.

concepts.title: The current selection is the task
concepts.text: Successful cat, grep and tail queries replace the selected result. After a correct filter, printing the whole log makes the result too broad; filter again to repair. find, show and help only inspect and leave it alone. Check example reads the current selected text, not command history. A no-match query displays a message and selects empty text; no grep exit-status model is taught here.

legacy_logs_teaching.example_description: Locate worker.log and select exactly its two FAIL lines. Keep their original order and exclude INFO/WARN messages and the unrelated audit log. This practice uses different files/messages/needle from the app.log/ERROR assignment.

files./var/log/worker.log:
11:00 INFO worker ready
11:01 FAIL task18 rejected
11:02 INFO retry queued
11:03 FAIL task27 expired
11:04 WARN queue growing
files./var/log/audit-practice.log:
11:00 INFO audit opened
11:05 FAIL unrelated audit warning

commands.explanation: Find the exact supplied basename; this fixed catalog form is not a recursive Tree search.
Read every line before deciding what to select.
Inspect recent messages; this omits an earlier FAIL, so refilter the full log afterward.
Select the two lines containing the literal uppercase FAIL.
An equivalent spaced pipeline; no extra command history is required.

legacy_logs_teaching.try_change: After success, run cat /var/log/worker.log and Check example. The selected text now includes INFO/WARN, so the current task fails. Repair with grep FAIL /var/log/worker.log (or the explained pipeline), then check again.

scenarios.title: Bring the service back
scenarios.summary: Repair a bad configuration and restore startup behavior.
scenarios.objective: Repair atlas to listen on port 8080, start it with that configuration, and enable it for boot.
steps: Inspect the unit and its journal. A legacy saved attempt may have no journal history; try starting it to record a diagnostic.
In the simulated /etc/atlas.conf editor, replace eighty with 8080 and choose Save configuration. The editor changes only this attempt.
Run each command separately and compare active with enabled.
hints: The saved port is a word. Use the simulated config editor to save a numeric port; running and enabled are separate.
Save 8080 in the editor, then restart atlas and enable it for boot.
scenarios.simplifications: Single modeled service, one configuration key. No unit dependency graph, privileges, socket binding, processes or actual boot.

guide.title: Inspect the failed start
guide.why: Status describes the unit; the journal explains recorded start failures. Enabling at boot and running now are independent.
guide.action: Inspect the unit and its journal. A legacy saved attempt may have no journal history; try starting it to record a diagnostic.

commands.explanation: Shows Loaded, Active and runtime information for the modeled unit.
Reads modeled unit events using journal-style output.

guide.title: Repair the saved configuration
guide.why: The port must be an integer from 1 through 65535. Saving a file does not reload a running service.
guide.action: In the simulated /etc/atlas.conf editor, replace eighty with 8080 and choose Save configuration. The editor changes only this attempt.

guide.title: Restart, enable, then verify
guide.why: Restart applies the saved port. Enable configures future boot startup but does not start the service.
guide.action: Run each command separately and compare active with enabled.

commands.explanation: Starts the service using the saved configuration.
Enables the unit for boot.
Checks whether it is running now.
Checks whether it is enabled for boot.

scenarios.explanation: The original word eighty is not a valid numeric port. Saving port=8080 repairs the file; restart loads that value into the running service. Enable is independent and makes the unit start at boot. A saved config edit alone does not change the currently loaded port.

service_teaching.prerequisite_note: No service-management experience is needed. Read this introduction or open the full assignment. The example keeps its own saved configuration, running service and command history.

concepts.title: A service works in the background
concepts.text: A service is a program that can keep working without an open terminal. This lab models a fictional service called atlas. Its configuration file holds a port number: a numbered entry point for an application. Here it is only a simulated value; no real program or socket is started.

concepts.title: Look for evidence before changing anything
concepts.text: systemctl status atlas reports whether atlas is running now and enabled for future boot. journalctl -u atlas reads recorded events for that service. A failed start can leave an explanation in the journal. Type one command in the terminal and press Enter or Run; its output appears above the input.

concepts.title: A saved file and a running program are different
concepts.text: Use the Port field in the simulated /etc/atlas.conf editor and choose Save configuration. The port must be a number from 1 to 65535 for atlas to start. Saving alone does not change a running service. Restart stops and starts atlas with the saved value; start does not reload a service that is already running.

concepts.title: Running now or starting with the computer
concepts.text: Enable records that a service should start when the computer starts (at boot); it does not start the service now. Restart or start controls whether it runs now. Verify both: is-active reports active when running, while is-enabled reports enabled for boot. In this lab, check both after repairing the configuration.

service_teaching.example_description: Try repairing a separate practice copy of atlas to use port 9090. Inspect its failed status and journal, put 9090 in the example editor, save, restart and enable it. Then verify both states. Use example port fills only the editor draft; it does not save or run anything.

commands.explanation: Inspect current activity and boot enablement before editing.
Read the saved diagnostic from the failed start.
Read the saved configuration; an unsaved editor draft is not this file.
Stop and start atlas using its saved configuration.
Enable future boot startup; this does not start atlas.
See whether atlas is running now.
See whether atlas is set to start when the computer starts.

service_teaching.try_change: After verifying the example, save port 9091 without restarting and inspect status: the running instance still uses 9090. Restart to load 9091, then check why it fails this example’s required port. Restore 9090 and restart. Finally try systemctl disable atlas: it can keep running while disabled for boot.

scenarios.title: Repair the internal DNS answer
scenarios.summary: Correct a record and reload the authoritative zone.
scenarios.objective: Make portal.lab.test resolve to 192.0.2.80 in the loaded authoritative zone.
steps: Read the zone and query the current answer.
In the simulated zone editor, repair the A record and enter a serial greater than the loaded serial. Save configuration; the running zone changes only after validation and reload.

seed_dns_teaching.prerequisite_note: Use the saved-versus-running idea from Bring the service back. This example has a different name, address and serial from your assignment.

concepts.title: A name and its A record
concepts.text: An A record associates a supplied host name with an IPv4 address. Here the authoritative answer is the value held by the serving copy of this one-record zone. There is no recursive lookup or cache.

concepts.title: Saved is not yet serving
concepts.text: Editing fields changes only an unsaved draft. Save configuration changes the saved record and serial. Queries still read the serving copy until you explicitly reload named. A validation result does not activate the change.

concepts.title: A larger serial before reload
concepts.text: A serial is a whole number from 0 through 4,294,967,295. You can save any value in that range, but this simplified exercise requires one larger than the loaded serial before reload. It does not model serial wrap arithmetic or secondary servers.

concepts.title: Read, save, validate, reload, query
concepts.text: cat /etc/named/lab.zone reads the saved record. dig asks for the serving answer. named-checkzone lab.test is a simulator-only abbreviated check; real BIND also needs a zone-file argument. systemctl reload named activates the saved example.

concepts.title: Use the supplied lowercase name
concepts.text: Real DNS name comparisons ignore ASCII letter case. This simplified exercise instead uses the supplied lowercase names as literal keys. Use mirror.lab.test in practice and the given assignment name later; this is a disclosed simulator limitation.

seed_dns_teaching.example_description: Repair mirror.lab.test from 198.51.100.4 to 198.51.100.44. It begins with saved and serving serial 41. Use the explained actions below; inserting settings or a command does not execute it.

scenarios.title: Recover the data volume
scenarios.summary: Fix a mount entry and free disposable capacity.
scenarios.objective: Make /data persistently reference /dev/vdb1, mount it read-write, and reduce usage to at most 80%. Only /data/cache is disposable.
steps: Inspect usage, disposable cache and the persistent mount entry.
Use the simulated /etc/fstab editor to correct the /data device. Save configuration, then remount the current volume read-write.
Remove only the marked cache and exercise the persistent mount.
hints: Cache cleanup requires a mounted writable filesystem. Removing it frees 300 MiB.
After the fstab repair and remount, rm -r /data/cache reduces usage to 650/1000 MiB.
scenarios.simplifications: Integer MiB capacity model, one filesystem, no inodes, UUID resolution, reserved blocks, open files or real devices. rm accepts only the explicitly disposable cache. Independent teaching practice uses a different device/capacity; its70% result does not change the existing80% goal. Unmount/mount is useful verification, not a grading-history requirement.

scenarios.explanation: The correct persistent data device is /dev/vdb1. A read-write mount permits removal of the 300 MiB disposable cache, leaving 650/1000 MiB used (65%). A successful unmount/mount cycle exercises the repaired fstab entry. Unmounting again makes the current objective incomplete.

seed_mount_teaching.prerequisite_note: Use the inspect, edit and verify method from Bring the service back. This example has a different known device and capacity from your assignment.

concepts.title: Volume, device and mountpoint
concepts.text: A volume is the supplied block of simulated storage. Its known device identifies it; /data is the place where it is mounted. This example never opens a real device or changes your computer.

concepts.title: Used capacity versus disposable cache
concepts.text: df -h reports the total and used MiB. du -sh /data/cache reports the only explicitly disposable data here. Removing 450 MiB from 1850 leaves 1400/2000 MiB, or 70%; the objective accepts usage at most 80%.

concepts.title: Saved pointer versus current mount
concepts.text: Save configuration edits only the simulated /etc/fstab pointer. It does not mount the volume or make it writable. Read cat /etc/fstab to compare that saved pointer with the supplied known device.

concepts.title: Cleanup needs read-write access
concepts.text: The current example begins mounted read-only. mount -o remount,rw /data makes that mount writable; then rm -r /data/cache can remove only the marked cache. No other deletion is supported.

concepts.title: Verify the saved entry and current state
concepts.text: umount /data makes the current volume unavailable. mount /data uses the saved device and restores read-write access if it is correct. This cycle is useful verification, not required to pass; the assignment is checked from its current state.

seed_mount_teaching.example_description: Recover the separate 2000 MiB example: known device /dev/vde2, saved wrong pointer /dev/vdf2, 1850 MiB used and 450 MiB disposable cache. Finish with the correct saved pointer, mounted read-write and no more than 80% used.
